summary: Prioritize dinosaur and everyday-physics topics like T. rex and car crumple zones, as they consistently drive the highest view counts and audience retention.
Draft titles that use direct, curiosity-inducing questions paired with relevant emojis (like 🦖 or 🚗) to boost initial click-through and engagement.
Formulate first-sentence hooks that make immediate, counter-intuitive claims or set up high-stakes scenarios rather than slow, generic introductions.
Keep video durations concise and punchy to maintain higher average view percentages and prevent audience drop-off in the middle seconds.
Avoid dry, overly academic phrasing in both titles and hooks in favor of direct second-person address ('You', 'Your') to capture viewer attention instantly.
winning_hooks: The real T. rex probably couldn't run. Not even a jog.
One T. rex bite pressed down like three small cars stacked on its teeth.
Your eyes are leaking right now, and your brain is hiding it.
You're a baby tyrannosaur, no bigger than a small dog.
A car that folds up in a crash keeps you safer than one that doesn't.
avoid: Slow, descriptive background introductions that take more than one sentence to get to the core point.
Niche or overly complex scientific topics without a relatable real-world comparison object like cars or animals.
Passive, low-energy statements in the opening hook that fail to challenge common assumptions.
next_experiment: A/B test two dinosaur-themed videos of identical length: one starting with a direct myth-busting statement as the hook, and the other starting with a direct question hook, while keeping titles and visual formatting constant.
